    Summary and Setup

    In two hands-on days you will write your own statistical model as a short R function, fit it with RTMB, check that the fit worked, compare it with other models and test its forecasts on years it never saw, using one tested recipe for each step and no proofs.

    This is a lesson in the style of Data Carpentry, built with The Carpentries Workbench. It is not an official Carpentries lesson. It was developed from the materials of the RTMB workshop hosted by the Pacific Salmon Commission in November 2026 (slides and examples by Paul van Dam-Bates).

    Who It Is For

    This lesson is for people who analyse data in R and fit regressions with lm() or glm(), and who now need a model that a formula interface cannot write for them:

    • a curve of their own;
    • a quantity that drifts over time;
    • groups that share information;
    • a forecast with an honest interval.

    It is also for people who must read and question such models, for example reviewers of stock assessments.

    The worked example is Fraser River sockeye salmon. The salmon background is explained from scratch, every recipe uses generic ingredients (dat, par, nll_*, fit_model()), and every episode has an “In Your Field” note for other kinds of data. The lesson is novice-level for model fitting, not for R. The learner profiles describe four people it was written for, from a stock assessment biologist to a public health analyst learning alone.

    If you are new to R, take an introductory R lesson first. If you already use TMB and want C++ or derivations, the Going Further page points to them.

    Prerequisite

    Before You Start

    You can:

    • open a project in RStudio or Positron and run a script;
    • read a CSV file and use filter() and mutate() from dplyr, and make a scatter or line plot with ggplot2 (with help);
    • make vectors and named lists (x[3], my_list$name), and write and call a short function;
    • use log() and exp();
    • say what a mean, a standard deviation and a normal (bell-shaped) distribution are;
    • read an estimate and its standard error from a regression.

    Not needed: calculus, matrix algebra, C++, TMB, Bayesian statistics, likelihood theory, fisheries science. The Data Carpentry lesson R for Ecologists, or any introductory R course, is enough.

    Not sure? Answer the three questions under “Before You Come” in the Setup instructions below.

    What You Will Leave With

    • Your own recipe box, my-recipes.R: every function the lesson teaches, typed by you.
    • A completed model report card for a stock you chose: data, fits, estimates, checks, model comparison and a tested forecast.
    • A template for your next analysis: the capstone template (capstone-template.R), a fill-in-the-blanks script for the whole workflow, on another stock or on your own data.
    • The one-page Recipe Index, which answers “Which recipe do I need?”.

    How the Lesson Works

    • The Quick Start runs the whole workflow first, in nine steps on one stock: data, model, fit, check the fit, estimates, check the model, random effect, compare, forecast.
    • Each later episode opens one of those steps and turns it into recipes you can reuse.
    • Most episodes include a “your turn” challenge on a second stock, Upper Pitt River, which fills in your report card one row at a time.
    • The capstone repeats the workflow on a stock you choose, or on your own data.

    From Episode 3 on, every episode opens with a Starting Point box that recreates everything it needs. You can therefore learn alone from this website, or rejoin after a missed session. Episode 10 (many stocks) is optional.

    About the Data

    The data are spawner and recruit estimates for 19 Fraser River sockeye salmon stocks, brood years 1948-2022, in thousands of fish. Spawners are the adult fish that spawned in a given year, called the brood year, and recruits are the adult offspring they produced. A stock is a group of salmon that spawn in the same place at the same time of year. The data were supplied with the Pacific Salmon Commission RTMB workshop and described there as not necessarily official numbers. The lesson also uses the North Pacific Gyre Oscillation index, a measure of ocean conditions. The script scripts/prepare-data.R in the lesson’s source repository records every cleaning step.

    These stocks matter to First Nations and to commercial and recreational fisheries. The lesson uses them to teach methods; nothing in it is management advice.

    The lesson follows the CARE principles for Indigenous data governance: collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics.

    Licence and attribution: to be confirmed with the data providers before the lesson is shared.

    Set up your computer before the workshop: it takes about 20 minutes, or longer if R has to compile the packages, as it may on Linux. At the end, a short script tells you whether everything works.

    Data Sets and Files

    Make a project folder (an RStudio or Positron project) with two subfolders, data/ and files/, and two empty scripts, my-recipes.R (your recipe box) and report-card.R (your report card). In RStudio, use File > New Project > New Directory > New Project. In Positron, make a new folder and open it with File > Open Folder.

    To download a file, right-click its link and choose Save Link As (in Safari, Download Linked File), save it in the folder shown, and check that its name has not gained a .txt ending.

    Download these two data files into data/:

    • the sockeye salmon data (sockeye.csv);
    • the ocean index data (npgo.csv).

    Download these three R scripts into files/:

    • the Quick Start script (quick-start.R), the whole Quick Start in one file, if you fall behind;
    • the finished recipe box (cookbook.R), every function the lesson teaches, used to catch up at the start of each episode;
    • the capstone template (capstone-template.R), used on Day 2.

    Your project folder should then look like this:

    my-project/
|-- data/
|   |-- npgo.csv
|   `-- sockeye.csv
|-- files/
|   |-- capstone-template.R
|   |-- cookbook.R
|   `-- quick-start.R
|-- my-recipes.R
`-- report-card.R

    Every path in the lesson, such as read.csv("data/sockeye.csv"), assumes that R is running in this project folder.

    The two data files. Spawners and recruits are in thousands of fish: 9.242 means 9242 fish.
    File Column Meaning Units
    sockeye.csv stock one of 19 Fraser River sockeye salmon stocks
    management_unit Early Stuart (1 stock), Early Summer (7), Summer (6), Late (5)
    brood_year year the parents spawned, 1948-2022 year
    spawners adults that spawned in the brood year thousands of fish
    recruits adult offspring produced by those spawners (caught or returning), all ages thousands of fish
    npgo.csv year calendar year, 1950-2026 year
    npgo North Pacific Gyre Oscillation index (ocean conditions; higher usually means more food) index (mean -0.18, SD 1.05)

    sockeye.csv has 1245 rows, with no zeros and no missing values. Some stocks start after 1948, and three stocks (Cultus, Portage and Scotch Creek) have missing brood years; every recipe in the lesson handles them.

    Software Setup

    You need:

    • the current version of R (4.5 or later), installed from CRAN, the R download site, not from Homebrew or conda;
    • RStudio Desktop or Positron;
    • the R packages RTMB, dplyr and ggplot2.

    CRAN keeps its ready-made Windows and macOS packages up to date only for the current version of R and the one before it. With an older R, you may get an old version of RTMB, or R may ask you to compile it. The lesson was tested with R 4.3.3, RTMB 2.0 and TMB 1.9.25. RTMB never compiles your models, so once the packages are installed you never need a compiler.

    Install the packages by running this in the R console (on Linux, read the Linux section below first):

    R 

    install.packages(c("RTMB", "dplyr", "ggplot2"))

    TMB is installed with RTMB. To find out which versions you have, run R.version.string and packageVersion("RTMB").

    R installs ready-made (binary) versions of RTMB, dplyr and ggplot2, so you do not need a compiler. If R asks “Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?”, answer no. If R offers RTMB only as a source package, update R instead of installing a compiler.

    R installs ready-made (binary) versions of RTMB, dplyr and ggplot2, so you do not need a compiler. If R asks “Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?”, answer no. If R offers RTMB only as a source package, update R instead of installing a compiler.

    CRAN has no ready-made packages for Linux, so by default R compiles RTMB and the other packages from their source code. Use Posit Package Manager instead: it has ready-made packages for Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat and SUSE. On Ubuntu 24.04, run this line before install.packages() (on Ubuntu 22.04, write jammy instead of noble):

    R 

    options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/__linux__/noble/latest"))

    For other systems, copy the repository line from the setup page of Posit Package Manager. The installation messages then say installing *binary* package.

    To compile the packages instead, first install the compilers and libraries R needs for this (on Debian or Ubuntu, run sudo apt install r-base-dev). Compiling RTMB, TMB, dplyr, ggplot2 and the packages they need takes 20 minutes or more, so do it before the workshop, not on the day.

    Check Your Setup

    Run this from your project folder. It must print Your setup works.

    Copy the code into a new script, save it in your project folder (for example as setup-check.R) and run all of it.

    R 

    library(RTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
sockeye <- read.csv("data/sockeye.csv")
npgo    <- read.csv("data/npgo.csv")
nll_check <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  -sum(dnorm(y, mean_y, exp(log_sd), log = TRUE))
}
dat_check <- list(y = log(sockeye$recruits / sockeye$spawners))
obj <- MakeADFun(function(p) nll_check(p, dat_check), list(mean_y = 0, log_sd = 0), silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
if (nrow(sockeye) == 1245 && nrow(npgo) == 77 && opt$convergence == 0) {
  cat("Your setup works.\n")
} else {
  cat("Something is wrong: see the Setup page.\n")
}

    OUTPUT 

    Your setup works.

    Loading dplyr also prints a message that some objects (filter, lag, intersect and others) are masked. That is normal.

    If the check does not print Your setup works.:

    • there is no package called 'RTMB' (or another package): run the install.packages() line again and read its messages.
    • cannot open the connection, with the warning cannot open file 'data/sockeye.csv': No such file or directory: R is not running in your project folder, or the file is not in data/. Open the project and try again.
    • Something is wrong: see the Setup page.: a data file is incomplete. Download both files again (sockeye.csv has 1245 rows and npgo.csv has 77).

    The Troubleshooting page lists other messages and what to do about them.

    Before You Come

    Answer these three questions without running R. They test the R and statistics the lesson assumes.

    1. What does f <- function(x, k = 2) x * k; f(c(1, 3)) print?
      1. 2 6; (b) 1 3 2; (c) an error; (d) 8.
    2. A regression slope is 0.50 with standard error 0.10. Which is the best reading?
      1. about 95% of the data lie between 0.3 and 0.7;
      2. a plausible range for the true slope is about 0.3 to 0.7;
      3. the slope is wrong by 0.10;
      4. 10% of the points are outliers.
    3. x <- list(a = 1, b = "z"). What does x$b return?
      1. 2 6. k takes its default value, 2, and x * k multiplies each element of the vector c(1, 3) by 2.
    2. (b). Plus or minus about two standard errors gives a plausible range for the slope itself (here 0.3 to 0.7). The standard error describes the estimate, not the spread of the data (a), it is not the size of the error (c), and it says nothing about outliers (d).
    3. "z". $ extracts the element named b from the list.

    If two of the three are hard, take an introductory R lesson first, such as Data Carpentry’s R for Ecologists.
